parakeet: Science believes there is no meaning is another projection. You'll often hear a claim like this. If science says there's no meaning, why even try? And at first glance, it sounds like a philosophical objection, but underneath it, it's just a projection, an assumption that science is offering a worldview in the same way religion does. It isn't. Science doesn't believe there is no meaning. In fact, science doesn't believe anything at all. Belief is not a part of the method. Science is a process, not a philosophy of life. And yet, scientists try anyway. They test ideas against reality. They measure what can be measured. They refine their models when they fail. They spend years, sometimes entire careers wrestling with uncertainty, ambiguity, and incomplete information, not because they expect guaranteed answers, but because understanding the world we live in is worth the effort. That pursuit alone should challenge the idea that science drains life of purpose. Meaning is not something science hands down. It doesn't arrive as a decree or doctrine. Meaning emerges through engagement, through curiosity, responsibility, creativity, and the willingness to confront reality as it actually is, not as we might wish it to be. And that kind of meaning is not fragile. It doesn't collapse when a model changes or a theory is refined. It doesn't depend on certainty or protection. It's earned through participation in the world, not withdrawal from it. When all is said and done, the irony at the center of the science versus religion debate is difficult to ignore.
